newsitem.title: UK: Britain offers 5,000 troops for new Bosnia force.
newsitem.headline: Britain offers 5,000 troops for new Bosnia force.

text.p: Britain said on Wednesday it was ready to contribute 5,000 heavily-armed ground troops to a new international peacekeeping force in Bosnia next year.
The Ministry of Defence said the troops would be part of a 31,000-strong "follow-on" force expected to replace the current NATO-led IFOR peace force, whose mandate expires at the end of next month.
Britain has around 8,000 heavily-armed troops in Bosnia as part of the 55,000-strong IFOR force.

The British contingent for the new force would be equipped with Challenger tanks, Scimitar armoured reconnaissance vehicles, track-mounted artillery and Warrior armoured fighting vehicles, a ministry spokesman said.
These ground forces would be backed up in the air by Harrier, Tornado and Jaguar combat aircraft, which would be ready to move to Bosnia at short notice from their bases in Britain and Germany.
"We are putting up 5,000 ground troops," the ministry spokesman said.

The commitment of forces by Defence Secretary Michael Portillo depended on what NATO planners ultimately decided would be necessary and the readiness of other nations to contribute to the new peacekeeping force.
NATO has in principle approved the new force although a final decision on its makeup is not expected for several weeks.
Britain will host an international conference on the civilian aspects of peace implementation in Bosnia on Wednesday and Thursday next week.
President Bill Clinton has already announced that the United States is ready to contribute to the follow-on force, but irritated his allies by failing to consult them in advance.

Clinton said after being re-elected earlier this month that he planned to send 8,500 troops to Bosnia for 18 months, with a a further 4-5,000 troops to be deployed to the region as possible reinforcements in an emergency.
British officials insisted on Tuesday that other countries who had agreed to supply troops for the new force had expected their tour of duty to be no more than 12 months.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, who is due to visit U.S. troops in Bosnia for Thanksgiving Day celebrations on Thursday, said the follow-on force could not guarantee peace in the former Yugoslav republic.
"The Bosnians themselves are going to have to make those changes," he said in Naples on Wednesday.
Germany is keen to send ground troops to Bosnia as part of the follow-on force, despite regional sensitivities dating back to the brutal Nazi occupation of Yugoslavia during World War Two.
